etymology: From New Thought / law-of-attraction teaching (popularized by The Secret, 2006, and re-boomed on social media in the 2020s): "manifesting" is speaking, visualizing, or journaling a desired outcome to make the universe deliver it.
biblical_def: Manifesting is the practice — now ambient in feeds, dorm rooms, and even some churches — of declaring, scripting, or visualizing a desired future on the theory that focused intention compels the universe to produce it. ("I'm manifesting the job"; vision boards; "lucky girl syndrome.") It is the old New Thought / law-of-attraction religion in app form, and its theology is specific even when its users are vague: an impersonal cosmos responsive to human will and words, with the self enthroned as the ordering power. The Christian observation must be equally specific. Scripture knows one Being whose words make worlds — and He is not us. The creature's posture toward the future is prayer, not decree: ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that (Jas 4:15); in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God (Phil 4:6). Prayer and manifesting are not cousins; they are opposite religions. Prayer bows to a Father who may say no for our good; manifesting issues work-orders to a cosmos that owes us. There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand (Prov 19:21).
webster_summary: Law-of-attraction practice (speak/visualize a desire so "the universe" delivers): New Thought religion in app form. The opposite of prayer — decree to a cosmos vs. petition to a Father (Jas 4:15; Phil 4:6). Verdict: reject.
webster_full: MANIFESTING, v./n. (Millennial / Gen-Z spiritual slang) Declaring, scripting, or visualizing a desired outcome to compel the universe to produce it.
Lineage: New Thought → law of attraction → The Secret (2006) → 2020s social-media boom (vision boards, scripting, "lucky girl syndrome").
Implied theology: an impersonal cosmos responsive to human intention; the self as ordering power.
Often imported into Christian vocabulary ("name it and claim it") with a verse attached.
Decode for parents: it is not prayer with extra steps; it is a rival religion with better marketing.
scriptures: Jas 4:15
For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.
Phil 4:6
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
Prov 19:21
There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand.
Matt 6:10
Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.
corruption_summary: Self-deification by vocabulary: the creature issuing decrees to the cosmos. Prayer and manifesting are opposite religions — petition to a sovereign Father versus work-orders to a universe that owes you.
corruption_paragraphs: The borrowed throne. Manifesting flatters the user with the one prerogative Scripture reserves to God: effectual speech over the future. He spake, and it was done (Psa 33:9) — that is a divine job description, not a human technique. When the practice migrates into church dress ("decree and declare," "speak it into existence"), the borrowed throne comes with it; word-of-faith religion is manifesting with a concordance. The biblical posture is unbending: the LORD's counsel stands, and ours bends to it — gladly, because His counsel is a Father's.

The pastoral edge. Manifesting also quietly crushes its practitioners: if outcomes track intention, then every unhealed illness and lost job is YOUR insufficient focus — a cruelty the gospel never deals. Prayer, by contrast, hands the outcome to wisdom and love higher than ours: thy will be done is not resignation but relief. Teach the young the difference between scripting a future and trusting a Father; one is a treadmill of self-blame, the other is rest.
roots_summary: New Thought → law of attraction → The Secret (2006) → 2020s social-media practice of decreeing desired futures; a rival religion to prayer — the self enthroned as ordering power.
roots_lines: New Thought movement (19th c.): mind as creative power
Law of attraction; The Secret (2006) mainstreams it
2020s social media: scripting, vision boards, "lucky girl syndrome"
Church-dress variant: "decree and declare," name-it-and-claim-it
Biblical contrast: If the Lord will (Jas 4:15); Thy will be done (Matt 6:10)
usage: "I'm manifesting that internship." — a work-order to a cosmos that owes nothing and isn't listening.
Prayer bows to a Father who may say no for our good; manifesting blames you when the universe doesn't ship.
He spake, and it was done (Psa 33:9) is a divine prerogative, not a morning routine.

etymology: Borrowed loosely from indigenous totem/guardian-spirit concepts and flattened by 2010s internet culture into a quip of identification: "coffee is my spirit animal," "she's my spirit animal."
biblical_def: In millennial usage, a spirit animal is whatever person, creature, or beverage one identifies with: a meme of kinship ("sloths are my spirit animal"). Two serious things hide under the joke. First, the borrowed metaphysics: the phrase is a flattened souvenir of actual pagan religion — totemism and guardian-spirit belief in which animals mediate spiritual identity and power. Most users mean nothing by it; but Christians, of all people, should decline even souvenir-grade paganism: what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils (1 Cor 10:20), and Israel was forbidden the whole family of spirit-traffic, divination, and enchantment (Deut 18:10-12). Romans 1 names the precise exchange the phrase jokes about: the glory of the incorruptible God traded for images of birds and fourfooted beasts (Rom 1:23). Second, the identity-hunger: the quip outsources self-understanding to a creature-mirror — tell me what I am like. Scripture answers the hunger higher: man is not defined by an animal familiar but by the image of God (Gen 1:27), given dominion OVER the beasts, and remade in Christ. You do not have a spirit animal; you have a Maker, and in Christ, an indwelling Spirit — and He is the Holy Ghost, not a sloth.
webster_summary: 2010s identification-quip ("coffee is my spirit animal") flattened from pagan totem/guardian-spirit religion; souvenir-grade spiritism plus identity outsourced to a creature-mirror. Gen 1:27 and Rom 1:23 answer both. Verdict: reject.
webster_full: SPIRIT ANIMAL, n. (Millennial slang, 2010s) A person, creature, or thing one humorously identifies with: "she's my spirit animal."
Flattened souvenir of totemism / guardian-spirit religion, in which animals mediate identity and power.
Usually meant as a joke; the metaphysics rides along anyway.
Identity-hunger underneath: self-understanding sought in a creature-mirror.
Decode for parents: harmless tone, borrowed paganism; Scripture assigns identity by image, not totem.
scriptures: Gen 1:27
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
Rom 1:23
And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things.
But I say, that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God: and I would not that ye should have fellowship with devils.
Deut 18:10
There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch,
corruption_summary: Souvenir paganism as a personality quiz: totem religion flattened into a quip, with identity outsourced to a creature-mirror — the Rom 1:23 exchange retold as a joke.
corruption_paragraphs: The souvenir problem. Nobody saying "tacos are my spirit animal" intends totemism — and that is rather the point: real spiritual categories get smuggled at the price of a laugh. A culture that jokes in the grammar of guardian spirits is a culture being slowly re-paganized below the level of argument; the New Age aisle did not shrink while the church laughed. Christians keep a cleaner tongue not from humorlessness but from jealousy for the only Spirit they confess.

The identity-mirror. The phrase's staying power is its second engine: people are starving to be told what they are. Horoscopes, personality acronyms, sorting-hat houses, spirit animals — one hunger, many mirrors. The gospel's answer outclasses them all: made in the image of God, given dominion over the creatures (not kinship under them), fallen, and in Christ renewed and indwelt by the Spirit Himself. Tell a believer searching the mirrors: your identity was assigned at creation and purchased at Calvary; no owl required.
roots_summary: Totem/guardian-spirit religion → 2010s internet quip of identification; souvenir paganism plus identity-hunger — answered by the image of God (Gen 1:27), not a creature-mirror.
roots_lines: Indigenous totem and guardian-spirit concepts (genuine pagan religion)
2010s internet flattens it into an identification meme
"X is my spirit animal" = humorous kinship claim
Underneath: spirit-traffic grammar (Deut 18) + identity-hunger
Biblical answer: image of God, dominion over creatures, the indwelling Holy Spirit
usage: "Honestly, raccoons are my spirit animal." — a joke wearing borrowed metaphysics.
One hunger, many mirrors: horoscopes, sorting quizzes, spirit animals — Gen 1:27 answers them all.
You have no totem; you have a Maker — and in Christ, the indwelling Spirit (1 Cor 6:19).

etymology: From the 2010 documentary Catfish and its MTV series: constructing a false online identity — fake photos, fabricated life — to lure someone into a relationship; by extension, any bait-and-switch self-presentation.
biblical_def: Catfishing is courtship by counterfeit: building a false identity online — borrowed photographs, invented careers, manufactured affection — to win a relationship the truth could not. The harvest is documented and bitter: victims defrauded of years, money, and trust; perpetrators hiding from their own faces. The Christian observation begins where Scripture always begins with disguise: the bait-and-switch is the devil's own signature move — Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light (2 Cor 11:14) — and every catfish is apprenticing, knowingly or not, in that school. The Bible even contains the form's prototype: Jacob wooed Rachel and woke to Leah — behold, it was Leah (Gen 29:25) — and the deceiving party's own history of disguise (Jacob in Esau's skins) came home to roost. Against the whole economy of constructed selves Scripture sets a plain command and a plainer hope. The command: putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour (Eph 4:25) — love that begins in a lie is not love but acquisition. The hope: the gospel is for unmasked people; you do not need a rented face to be loved, because the One who sees the real face already went to a cross for it.
webster_summary: Courtship by counterfeit: a fabricated online identity deployed to win love the truth couldn't. The devil's signature move (2 Cor 11:14), prototyped at Leah's veil (Gen 29:25); love that begins in a lie is acquisition. Verdict: reject.
webster_full: CATFISHING, n./v. (Millennial / internet slang, from the 2010 documentary Catfish) Constructing a false online identity to lure someone into a relationship.
Tools: borrowed photos, invented biography, manufactured affection.
Extended sense: any bait-and-switch self-presentation (profiles "catfish" mildly by curation).
Documented harvest: defrauded years, money, and trust; perpetrators hiding from their own faces.
Decode for parents: teach your kids both halves — don't be the counterfeit, and verify before you trust.
scriptures: And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.
And it came to pass, that in the morning, behold, it was Leah: and he said to Laban, What is this thou hast done unto me? did not I serve with thee for Rachel? wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?
Eph 4:25
Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.
Prov 26:24
He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him;
corruption_summary: The constructed self weaponized: identity-fraud for affection. Love that begins in a lie is acquisition, and every disguise apprentices in the angel-of-light school.
corruption_paragraphs: The school of disguise. Catfishing is only the felony-grade end of a spectrum the whole platform economy encourages: filtered faces, curated lives, personalities A/B-tested for engagement. Where every profile is a little fiction, the full counterfeit stops feeling like a different KIND of thing — just more of the same. The Christian draws the line at the root: we are members one of another (Eph 4:25), and a self presented for relationship must be the self that shows up. Curate modesty, not fiction.

Unmasked and loved anyway. The catfish's engine is usually not malice first but shame: the conviction that the real face, the real body, the real résumé could never be loved. The gospel speaks directly into that engine: God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners — the unfiltered worst already known — Christ died for us. A person secure in that has no use for a rented identity; and a church full of such people should be the one community where masks are unnecessary.
roots_summary: From the 2010 Catfish documentary: false online identity deployed to win a relationship; the angel-of-light maneuver (2 Cor 11:14) in dating-app form, prototyped at Leah's veil.
roots_lines: Catfish (2010 documentary) and MTV series name the practice
Method: borrowed photos, invented biography, manufactured affection
Spectrum: from filtered curation to full identity-fraud
Biblical prototype: Jacob beguiled with Leah (Gen 29:25)
Signature lineage: Satan transformed into an angel of light (2 Cor 11:14)
usage: "Three months of texting and the photos were a Brazilian model's — classic catfish."
Love that begins in a lie is not love but acquisition; speak truth with thy neighbour (Eph 4:25).
The gospel retires the rented face: the real one was already loved at the cross.

etymology: From internet slang thirst (visible craving for attention or desire) + trap: a photo or video posted deliberately to provoke desire and harvest its attention — named, with rare honesty, by the very culture that posts them.
biblical_def: A thirst trap is a post engineered to provoke desire: the gym mirror shot, the swimsuit angle, the caption performing obliviousness ("just woke up like this") — bait set for the eyes, with the harvested attention as the catch. The slang itself is a small confession: the culture that posts them named them traps. The Christian observation handles both ends of the line. To the one posting: Scripture treats the deliberate provocation of desire outside covenant as real harm done to real souls — woe to that man by whom the offence cometh (Matt 18:7) — and it names the engine honestly: a thirst for being wanted, fed in a way that can never fill it. Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised (Prov 31:30) — and the same ledger holds for men flexing for the feed. The hidden man of the heart... a meek and quiet spirit... in the sight of God of great price (1 Pet 3:4) is not a consolation prize; it is the only currency that appreciates. To the one scrolling: the trap only works on the unguarded; covenant your eyes (Job 31:1) and starve the economy. Bodies are temples, not billboards (1 Cor 6:19-20).
webster_summary: A post engineered to provoke desire and harvest attention — named "trap" by its own culture. Matt 18:7 weighs the snare-setter; Prov 31:30 and 1 Pet 3:4 re-price the currency; Job 31:1 guards the scroller. Verdict: reject.
webster_full: THIRST TRAP, n. (Millennial / Gen-Z slang) A photo or video posted deliberately to provoke desire and collect its attention.
Thirst = visible craving; trap = bait set for the eyes.
Standard forms: gym mirror shot, swimsuit angle, faux-oblivious caption.
The culture's own name for it is a confession: a snare, set on purpose.
Decode for parents: the engine is a hunger to be wanted; re-price the currency before the algorithm does.
scriptures: Prov 31:30
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
1 Pet 3:4
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
Matt 18:7
Woe unto the world because of offences! for it must needs be that offences come; but woe to that man by whom the offence cometh!
Job 31:1
I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?
corruption_summary: Desire-bait as a personal economy: the body posted as billboard, attention harvested as worth. The culture's own word confesses the snare; Scripture weighs the setter and re-prices the currency.
corruption_paragraphs: The economy of being wanted. The thirst trap monetizes a real hunger — to be desired, noticed, confirmed — and pays it in the one currency that inflates to worthlessness: anonymous appetite. Every harvest requires a bigger bait; the metric rises as the soul empties. Scripture re-prices from outside the market: the fear of the LORD praised over deceitful favour, the hidden person of great price in God's sight. That is not modesty as repression; it is modesty as refusing to sell below value.

The snare-setter's ledger. The age treats provoked desire as the viewer's problem alone; the Lord's woe falls also on the one BY WHOM the offence cometh (Matt 18:7), and the apostolic standard for dress is shamefacedness — that older word for a glory that doesn't bait (1 Tim 2:9). Christians keep both commands in the same pocket: post nothing as bait, and covenant the eyes against the bait of others (Job 31:1). Bodies are temples, purchased at price; temples are not billboards (1 Cor 6:19-20).
roots_summary: Internet thirst (craving for attention) + trap: a post engineered to provoke desire and harvest attention; the culture's own name confesses the snare (Matt 18:7).
roots_lines: Internet slang thirst: visible craving for attention or desire
+ trap: bait set deliberately for the eyes
Standard forms: gym mirror, swimsuit angle, faux-oblivious caption
Economy: desire provoked → attention harvested → worth inflated away
Biblical re-pricing: Prov 31:30; 1 Pet 3:4; Job 31:1; 1 Cor 6:19-20
usage: "It's not a thirst trap, it's a fit check" — the caption performing obliviousness is part of the trap.
Anonymous appetite is a currency that inflates to nothing; the hidden person is of great price (1 Pet 3:4).
Two pockets, one standard: post no bait, and covenant the eyes (Job 31:1).

etymology: From pose; sharpened in 1980s-90s skate, punk, and metal subcultures: one who adopts the look of a scene without its substance — the kid with the untouched skateboard and the flawless band shirt.
biblical_def: A poser is a counterfeit belonger: someone wearing a subculture's uniform without paying its dues — the pristine skateboard carried but never ridden, the band shirt without a single album heard. Gen X coined it as a tribal verdict, and beneath the gatekeeping sneer sits a moral instinct Scripture takes with total seriousness: the difference between appearing and being. The Lord's own ministry was one long campaign against religious posers — hypocrites praying on corners to be seen of men (Matt 6:5), whited sepulchres outwardly beautiful and inwardly dead (Matt 23:27-28) — and the apostolic warning generalizes it: if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself (Gal 6:3). The decode for the church is uncomfortable and healthy: every congregation risks a Christianity of merch — the verse-tattoo, the worship-brand hoodie, the fluent vocabulary — with no rides on the board. Let love be without dissimulation (Rom 12:9). The old skaters' cure was also roughly biblical: nobody called you a poser who had seen you fall and get up; substance is proven by scars, not gear. Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith.
webster_summary: Gen X verdict for a counterfeit belonger — the look without the substance. Scripture's category exactly: hypocrites, whited sepulchres, the man who thinks himself something and is nothing (Gal 6:3). Verdict: examine — starting with the mirror.
webster_full: POSER, n. (Gen X slang, 1980s-90s skate/punk/metal) One who adopts a scene's look without its substance.
Field marks: the untouched skateboard, the flawless band shirt, fluent jargon with no dues paid.
A tribal gatekeeping word — but the moral instinct under it is sound.
Biblical category: appearing vs. being; the hypocrite's whole portfolio.
Decode for parents (and elders): churches grow posers too — merch-deep Christianity with no rides on the board.
scriptures: Matt 6:5

And when thou prayest, thou shalt not be as the hypocrites are: for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
Matt 23:28
Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.
Gal 6:3
For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself.
Rom 12:9
Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.
corruption_summary: The look without the life — and the church is not exempt: a Christianity of merch and vocabulary with no scars is the religious poser the Lord rebuked in every chapter of Matthew 23.
corruption_paragraphs: The merch-deep disciple. Every scene the world builds gets its posers, and so does the kingdom: the right hoodie, the right podcast vocabulary, the testimony polished for the open mic — and a private life the gear has never touched. The Lord's anatomy of it is unimproved after twenty centuries: outwardly beautiful, inwardly unvisited (Matt 23:27). The examination is not whether one wears the gear but whether one has ever bled in it: prayed unseen, repented expensively, obeyed when it cost.

The gatekeeper's own mirror. Gen X wielded "poser" as a status weapon, and that half does not survive Scripture: judging the authenticity of others is the fastest way to become inauthentic oneself (Matt 7:3-5). The biblical use of the category points inward first — examine YOURSELVES, whether ye be in the faith (2 Cor 13:5) — and then turns outward not in sneering but in discipleship: the cure for a poser was always an older skater willing to teach him to actually ride.
roots_summary: From pose; 1980s-90s skate/punk verdict for the look-without-substance belonger; Scripture's hypocrite category exactly — aimed first at the mirror (2 Cor 13:5).
roots_lines: From pose: a posture held for appearance
1980s-90s skate, punk, and metal subcultures sharpen the verdict
Field marks: pristine gear, fluent jargon, no dues
Biblical category: hypocrite, whited sepulchre (Matt 23)
Cure: scars over gear — and an older rider willing to teach
usage: "Nice deck. Ever ridden it?" — the poser test, c. 1989.
Churches grow posers too: merch-deep faith with no rides on the board (Matt 23:28).
Aim the category at the mirror first: examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith (2 Cor 13:5).

pos: adjective (Gen X slang; older American origin)
etymology: American English (early 1800s), originally a counterfeiter's machine and then counterfeit money itself; revived by 1980s-90s youth culture (surf/skate/Bill-and-Ted register) for anything fake, unfair, or wrong: "that's totally bogus."
biblical_def: Bogus began its career in literal counterfeiting — the name of a machine that struck fake coins — and spent the 1980s-90s as Gen X's all-purpose verdict on the fake and the unfair. As slang goes, it is a keeper: a one-word protest that some things are NOT the real article, spoken by a generation otherwise marinated in irony. The Christian observation: Scripture is intensely interested in counterfeits and entirely on the side of calling them out. The LORD's commercial law is the original anti-bogus statute — a false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight (Prov 11:1). And the New Testament extends the category from coinage to spiritual goods, warning of bogus apostles (false apostles, deceitful workers, 2 Cor 11:13), bogus gospels (Gal 1:6-9), and bogus spirits to be tested rather than trusted: believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God (1 John 4:1). A church that has lost the nerve to say "bogus" — to name the counterfeit AS counterfeit — has lost a tool of love, for the counterfeit always defrauds someone. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good (1 Thess 5:21): test the coin, keep the gold, and say plainly which is which.
webster_summary: From a counterfeiter's machine (1800s) to Gen X's verdict on the fake and unfair. A keeper: Scripture is anti-counterfeit from Prov 11:1 to 1 John 4:1 — test the coin, keep the gold, say which is which. Verdict: redeemable.
webster_full: BOGUS, adj. (American, early 1800s; Gen X revival 1980s-90s) Counterfeit; fake; unfair; wrong: "that's totally bogus."
Original sense: a counterfeiter's coin-striking machine, then the fake money itself.
Gen X register: surf/skate/Bill-and-Ted — the all-purpose protest of the fake.
A rare slang keeper: a one-word defense of the real article.
Biblical kin: false balances, false apostles, false spirits — all to be named.
scriptures: Prov 11:1
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ.
1 John 4:1
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
1 Thess 5:21
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
corruption_summary: Little corruption in the word itself — it IS the anti-corruption verdict. The danger is the culture's loss of nerve to use it: a generation taught that authenticity-judgments are intolerant stops naming counterfeits, and the counterfeits collect.
corruption_paragraphs: The verdict the age forbids. Relativism's only forbidden sentence is "that is fake" — bogus gospels, bogus identities, bogus spiritualities all claim equal shelf space, and discernment itself gets renamed judgmentalism. But Scripture commands the testing of spirits and the proving of all things precisely because counterfeits defraud the people who receive them. Calling bogus is not unkindness; it is consumer protection for souls.

The word itself is largely innocent; the principle to keep is the just weight. God's delight in true balances (Prov 11:1) reaches past the marketplace to every representation a man makes — his promises, his books, his gospel. The Christian should be the least bogus thing in any room: true coin all the way through, and therefore free to test every other coin without fear. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
roots_summary: Counterfeiter's machine (1800s) → counterfeit money → Gen X verdict on the fake and unfair; a slang keeper that matches Scripture's anti-counterfeit grain (Prov 11:1; 1 John 4:1).
roots_lines: American English, early 1800s: a counterfeiter's coin machine
Extends to the counterfeit money itself
1980s-90s Gen X revival: fake, unfair, wrong — "totally bogus"
A one-word protest on behalf of the real article
Biblical kin: false balance, false apostles, false spirits — all named
usage: "They changed the rules after we paid? Bogus." — the just-weight instinct in one word.
Relativism forbids exactly one sentence — "that is fake" — and Scripture commands it (1 John 4:1).
Be the least bogus thing in the room: true coin through, free to test every other (1 Thess 5:21).

etymology: American slang (1960s-on) for the television: boob (a fool) + tube (the cathode-ray tube) — the fool-maker box; the name a whole culture gave its own favorite appliance.
biblical_def: The boob tube is the television, named with startling self-awareness: the tube that boobifies — the appliance a generation accused, even while watching it, of making fools. (Companion coinage: the idiot box.) The Gen X childhood was scheduled around it; the Boomer living room was furnished toward it; and the smartphone has since put one in every pocket and called it progress. The Christian observation honors the old joke by taking it seriously. Scripture's media-law is written in eye-grammar: I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes (Psa 101:3); the light of the body is the eye (Matt 6:22) — what streams in through that gate furnishes the whole house. And its time-law prices the hours the tube consumes: walk circumspectly... redeeming the time, because the days are evil (Eph 5:15-16). The issue was never the cathode ray; it is the passive, endless, appetite-led intake that the nickname confessed — hours of unchosen images flowing into an unguarded gate. The cure is as old as the joke: choose what enters (Phil 4:8 — whatsoever things are true, honest, just, pure), price the hours, and keep the best seat in the house aimed at faces, not screens.
webster_summary: The television, self-accusingly named the fool-maker box (1960s-on). The old joke states the biblical case: guard the eye-gate (Psa 101:3; Matt 6:22) and price the hours (Eph 5:16) — now that the tube lives in every pocket. Verdict: examine.
webster_full: BOOB TUBE, n. (American slang, 1960s-on) The television: boob (fool) + tube (cathode-ray) — the fool-maker box.
Companion coinage: the idiot box; a culture's self-aware verdict on its favorite appliance.
Gen X childhood scheduled around it; the smartphone since multiplied it into every pocket.
The accusation was never the hardware but the passive, appetite-led intake.
Decode across generations: the tube won the argument by miniaturizing; the eye-gate laws still apply.
scriptures: I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me.
Matt 6:22
The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
Eph 5:16
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
Phil 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
corruption_summary: A culture's self-accusation, ignored by the accusers: the fool-maker box watched by the hour anyway — and now miniaturized into every pocket with the autoplay set to ON.
corruption_paragraphs: The joke that lost. A society that names its appliance the boob tube and then organizes its evenings around it has confessed and continued in the same breath — the pattern of every besetting habit. The honest old nickname has since been retired, not because the intake got nobler but because the device got personal: nobody calls the phone an idiot box, though it runs the same passive feed with better targeting. Keeping the old name's honesty is half the battle.

The guarded gate and the priced hour. Scripture will not let the matter rest at sneering or at abstinence-pride; it legislates the gate and the clock. The gate: set no wicked thing before the eyes, think on the true and the pure (Psa 101:3; Phil 4:8) — chosen intake, not ambient intake. The clock: the days are evil and the hours are owed (Eph 5:16); the question for any screen is what it is purchasing with a life's evenings. A man's feed and his queue are discipleship documents; read them as such.
roots_summary: 1960s self-accusing nickname for television (boob = fool + cathode tube); the joke states the biblical case — guard the eye-gate, price the hours — now that the tube is pocket-sized.
roots_lines: American slang, 1960s-on: boob (fool) + tube (cathode-ray)
Companion: the idiot box — a culture's verdict on its own appliance
Gen X childhood scheduled around it; Boomers furnished rooms toward it
The smartphone miniaturized the tube into every pocket, autoplay ON
Eye-gate and time laws: Psa 101:3; Matt 6:22; Eph 5:16; Phil 4:8
usage: "Turn off the boob tube and go outside" — the most biblical sentence of 1985.
Nobody calls the phone an idiot box; it earned the title with better targeting.
A man's queue is a discipleship document: whatsoever things are pure, think on these (Phil 4:8).

etymology: 1960s catchphrase from soul music (Aretha Franklin's "Respect" backing vocals, 1967) and the TV sketch show Rowan & Martin's Laugh-In (1968-73), where saying it triggered a bucket of water or a trapdoor: "give it to me straight / let me have it."
biblical_def: Sock it to me is the Boomer era's grinning invitation to let-me-have-it: born in soul music's call for full-strength delivery and immortalized on Laugh-In, where the phrase summoned the pie, the bucket, or the trapdoor — famously even from a presidential candidate gamely asking "Sock it to ME?" It is innocent furniture of a generation's youth, and the dictionary receives it as such: a time to laugh (Eccl 3:4) covers a great deal of 1968. But tucked inside the catchphrase is a posture worth keeping: the willingness to be hit with it straight — full strength, no padding. Scripture commends exactly that appetite when the payload is truth: let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness: and let him reprove me; it shall be an excellent oil (Psa 141:5); faithful are the wounds of a friend (Prov 27:6); and the wise man, rebuked, loves you for it (Prov 9:8). A generation that asked for it straight on the comedy stage often padded everything else — and ours pads more. The believer keeps the old phrase's nerve where it counts: open Bible, trusted friend, plain words — sock it to me.
webster_summary: 1960s soul/Laugh-In catchphrase: "let me have it, full strength." Innocent era-furniture — and a posture worth keeping when the payload is truth: let the righteous smite me (Psa 141:5). Verdict: neutral.
webster_full: SOCK IT TO ME, catchphrase (Boomer era, 1960s) "Give it to me straight; let me have it" — full-strength delivery invited.
Soul lineage: Aretha Franklin's "Respect" (1967) backing vocals.
TV lineage: Laugh-In (1968-73), where the phrase triggered the bucket, pie, or trapdoor.
Famously delivered as a question by a 1968 presidential candidate on the show.
Innocent era-furniture; the keep-worthy core is the appetite for unpadded truth.
scriptures: Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness: and let him reprove me; it shall be an excellent oil, which shall not break my head: for yet my prayer also shall be in their calamities.
Prov 27:6
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
Prov 9:8
Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee.
Eccl 3:4
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
corruption_summary: No corruption to speak of — era-furniture from the comedy stage. The recoverable core is the posture it performs: invite the hit, full strength, when the payload is truth.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry is innocent period slang; the principle to recover is the unpadded ear. The phrase performed, as comedy, what Scripture prescribes as wisdom: stand still and receive it full strength. The Psalmist asks the righteous to smite him and calls it kindness; Proverbs prices a friend's wounds above an enemy's kisses. The man who can genuinely say "sock it to me" to his Bible, his wife, and his elders — and not flinch into self-defense — possesses a rarer asset than any in his portfolio.

The padded age. Every generation since has added bubble wrap: feedback became sandwiched, criticism became violence, and the algorithm now curates a world that never socks anything to anyone. The result is not safety but fragility — souls that shatter at the first unfiltered sentence. The old catchphrase, grinning from 1968, is a small rebuke to all of it: ask for it straight, laugh when the bucket falls, and let the righteous smite you; it is oil, not injury.
roots_summary: Soul music ("Respect," 1967) and Laugh-In (1968-73) catchphrase: "let me have it, full strength" — innocent era-furniture whose keep-worthy core is the unpadded ear (Psa 141:5).
roots_lines: Soul lineage: backing vocals of Aretha Franklin's "Respect" (1967)
Laugh-In (1968-73): the phrase summons bucket, pie, or trapdoor
A 1968 presidential candidate delivers it as a question on air
Sense: give it to me straight; full-strength delivery invited
Keep-worthy core: faithful are the wounds of a friend (Prov 27:6)
usage: "Sock it to me!" — and down came the bucket; 1968's entire comedic economy.
The posture outlives the punchline: invite the hit when the payload is truth (Psa 141:5).
A padded age could use one grinning phrase that asks for it straight.

etymology: From 1930s blues/jazz ("truckin'" as a dance and keep-moving idiom) revived by R. Crumb's 1968 one-page comic of strutting big-footed walkers; through the 1970s it meant: persist, keep going, carry on through the grind.
biblical_def: Keep on truckin' is the Boomer era's one-line theology of persistence: whatever the road serves up, keep moving. Born in 1930s blues idiom and rebooted by R. Crumb's strutting 1968 cartoon — plastered across vans, t-shirts, and mudflaps for a decade — it functioned as a grinning, secular benediction: don't quit. The dictionary receives this one warmly, because its instinct is among the most biblical in all of slang. Scripture's ethics of the long road are exactly this, with the engine named: let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not (Gal 6:9); let us run with patience the race that is set before us (Heb 12:1); I press toward the mark (Phil 3:14); and the old man's victory lap, I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course (2 Tim 4:7). The one correction the gospel makes to the mudflap is the fuel source: the believer's truckin' is not gritted-teeth self-propulsion but looking unto Jesus (Heb 12:2), strength supplied by the One who never wearies (Isa 40:28-31). Direction matters too — persistence on the broad road is just efficient ruin. Point the truck at the mark, then by all means: keep on.
webster_summary: Blues idiom + R. Crumb's 1968 comic: the era's grinning benediction of persistence. Nearly straight Bible — Gal 6:9, Heb 12:1, Phil 3:14 — once the fuel (looking unto Jesus) and the direction are set. Verdict: redeemable.
webster_full: KEEP ON TRUCKIN', catchphrase (Boomer era; blues 1930s, revived 1968) Persist; keep going; carry on through the grind.
Blues/jazz lineage: "truckin'" as a dance and keep-moving idiom (1930s).
R. Crumb's 1968 one-page comic of strutting walkers makes it a decade's emblem.
Vans, t-shirts, mudflaps: the 1970s' secular benediction.
Gospel corrections: fuel (looking unto Jesus) and direction (the mark, not the broad road).
scriptures: Gal 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
Phil 3:14
I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
2 Tim 4:7
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
corruption_summary: Scarcely corrupted — the rare slang whose instinct is nearly straight Bible. The two gospel amendments: persistence needs a fuel source better than grit, and a direction better than the broad road.
corruption_paragraphs: Grit and its limits. The mudflap version runs on self-propulsion, and self-propulsion runs out — ask any Boomer who white-knuckled the long road into burnout or a bottle. The biblical long-haul has a named engine: they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength... they shall walk, and not faint (Isa 40:31), and the race is run looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher (Heb 12:2). Perseverance of the saints is not the saints' grip on God but God's grip on the saints — which is why it actually finishes.

Largely innocent era-slang; the principle to add is direction. Persistence is a multiplier, not a virtue by itself: keep on truckin' down the broad way and you merely arrive at destruction ahead of schedule (Matt 7:13). Scripture's persistence verses all carry a vector — well doing, the race SET BEFORE US, the mark, the faith KEPT. Point the truck first; then the old benediction is gospel: in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
roots_summary: 1930s blues idiom revived by R. Crumb's 1968 comic into the 1970s' benediction of persistence; nearly straight Bible (Gal 6:9; Heb 12:1) once fuel and direction are gospel-set.
roots_lines: 1930s blues/jazz: "truckin'" as dance and keep-moving idiom
R. Crumb's one-page comic (1968): the strutting big-footed walkers
1970s ubiquity: vans, t-shirts, mudflaps
Sense: persist; carry on through the grind
Gospel engine and vector: Isa 40:31; Heb 12:1-2; Phil 3:14
usage: "Rough year. Keep on truckin'." — the mudflap benediction, half a Bible verse already.
Grit runs out; they that wait upon the LORD renew their strength (Isa 40:31).
Persistence is a multiplier — point the truck at the mark first (Phil 3:14).

etymology: American slang for the police (recorded by the 1920s-30s, mainstreamed in the 1960s-70s counterculture); origin disputed — possibly from "fuss" (those who make the fuss) or a mocking softening of "the force."
biblical_def: The fuzz is the Boomer-and-after nickname for the police — mild as cop-slang goes (far gentler than what followed it), carrying a smirk rather than a snarl: authority as nuisance, the party's natural predator. ("Cheese it, the fuzz!") The dictionary decodes the smirk with both Testaments open. Scripture's doctrine of the civil officer is loftier than the nickname and sterner than the badge: the powers that be are ordained of God, and the magistrate is the minister of God to thee for good... a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil (Rom 13:1, 4); submit yourselves... for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well (1 Pet 2:13-14). The believer therefore cannot adopt contempt-for-the-office as a personality, even a twinkling one; honor is commanded, and the man in the cruiser bears, however imperfectly, a delegated sword. The same chapters bound the office: ministers OF GOD have a Master, their sword is FOR GOOD, and officers who turn the sword against the innocent answer to the Judge of all the earth — as Scripture's own narratives of corrupt authority show. Honor the office, obey the lawful, appeal the unjust like Paul did (Acts 22:25; 25:11) — and keep the smirk off the uniform God ordained.
webster_summary: Counterculture-era nickname for the police: authority-as-nuisance with a smirk. Rom 13 and 1 Pet 2 decode it: the office is God-ordained and owed honor; the office-holder is bounded, answerable, and appealable. Verdict: examine.
webster_full: THE FUZZ, n. collect. (recorded 1920s-30s; mainstream 1960s-70s) The police; authority as nuisance: "cheese it, the fuzz!"
Mild as cop-slang goes — a smirk, not a snarl; the party's natural predator.
Origin disputed: perhaps from "fuss," perhaps a mocking softening of "the force."
Counterculture register: the era's reflexive wink at the badge.
Decode: Scripture out-ranks both the smirk and the badge — ordained office, bounded officer.
scriptures: Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Or unto governors, as unto them that are sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well.
Titus 3:1
Put them in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates, to be ready to every good work,
corruption_summary: A smirk at the badge that, practiced long enough, becomes a doctrine: authority as such read as nuisance. Scripture honors the ordained office, bounds the office-holder, and forbids contempt as a personality.
corruption_paragraphs: Contempt as a reflex. The wink in "the fuzz" trained a generation — and its children, with harder words — to file lawful authority under nuisance by default. Romans 13 will not file it there: the officer on the corner participates, however humanly, in an office God ordained for the good of the innocent and the terror of the violent. A believer may joke; he may not curate contempt. The reflexive sneer at the badge is, at bottom, a sneer at the Orderer behind all order.

The bounded badge. The same passage that commands honor also reads the officer his commission: minister OF GOD, FOR GOOD, against EVILDOERS — three boundary stakes. Authority that turns the sword on the innocent has left its warrant, and Scripture models the response: Paul invoked his rights (Acts 22:25), appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11), and obeyed God rather than men where commands crossed (Acts 5:29) — all without one syllable of cop-contempt. Honor the office, hold the office-holder to it, and teach your sons to do both at a traffic stop.
roots_summary: 1920s-30s cop-slang mainstreamed by the 1960s-70s counterculture: the police as smirked-at nuisance; decoded by Rom 13 / 1 Pet 2 — ordained office, bounded officer, commanded honor.
roots_lines: Recorded by the 1920s-30s in American slang
Mainstreamed by the 1960s-70s counterculture

Register: a smirk at the badge — authority as nuisance
Scripture's frame: ordained office (Rom 13:1), bounded sword (Rom 13:4), appealable (Acts 25:11)
usage: "Cheese it — the fuzz!" — the 1960s party's fire alarm.
Joke if you must; curate no contempt: the powers that be are ordained of God (Rom 13:1).
Honor the office, hold its holder to the warrant, and appeal like Paul (Acts 25:11).
